done.why: I died a fourth time. I dropped my only light in the Damp Passage so I could fetch it later through the vista, then walked out into the dark Junction, and a grue got me twice in a row. The old man had already warned me he didn't have a fourth revival left, and he was right. I ended up in a Void where nothing further will happen.

about: An old, ageless man sets you a final test at the bottom of an endless stair. You go around his ruined underground empire collecting the things he carries in your dreams: an amulet from the bottom of an icy lake, a staff from a crook at a cliff, a ring smuggled out of the past in a time machine, a book from the sliding-wall Royal Puzzle, and a hood and cloak taken from a shadow that turns out to have your own face. Once you have proved yourself, you go down to meet him. A lot of it is about letting go: you can't carry a light across the lake, and you win the shadow fight by not finishing it.

ending.what: A losing ending. After my fourth death the voice said 'perhaps it has been another that I have been seeking. Good night, oh worthy adventurer!' and left me in the Void. Before that I had the amulet, ring, staff, book, sword, hood and cloak, and the secret door down to the old man was open. It still turned me back because I hadn't yet been everywhere I needed to go: the grue-dark passage past the lake and the spray can in room 8.

moments.note: The man at the cliff hauls the chest up, and then for several turns you only hear him: the lock being tried, coins counted twice. He made me wait, and the waiting had character.
The viking ship came past exactly once while I was mindlessly typing wait. It's gone for good and I never worked out what I was meant to say.
The lake shore spells out plainly that a lamp won't survive the water and that worn things stay with you. A clear rule I could plan around.
Touching the vista table at IV put me on a sacrificial altar and I was killed at once. The old man's prison-cell revival afterwards was eerie.
Vista II showed a spray can in room 8, but I arrived in pitch darkness because my torch had been scattered to the other side of the lake when I died.
Realising I could push the time machine into the Jewel Room so I would arrive in the past already inside the locked room. That was a real aha.
Waiting in 776 got me vaporized by a guard with a waffle. The timing felt random: the same waiting had been safe on my first visit.
Hiding the ring under the seat of the machine and finding it there 172 years later. Very satisfying.
Two different sandstone blocks seemed to carry ladders. I needed the ladder examine text to work out that a ladder block had to sit right beside the hole.
The book was in a niche hidden under a sliding block I had walked past many times. Finding it by accident was delightful.
Climbing out of the Royal Puzzle after planning an 18-push route on paper in my head.
The sword from the rock appears in my hand when the hooded figure shows up. And under the hood it has my face.
The secret stair turned me back with a long paragraph saying I wasn't ready. Clear, but it only said 'places you have not yet been', with no pointer to which ones.

I walked into the dark Junction without a light because I'd dropped the torch in the Damp Passage on purpose. A grue ate me, and again one step later. My own carelessness, but the run ended permanently.

wished: I wished the viking ship had come round a second time, or that its hint had landed before it left.
I wished I could get the torch back to the west side of the lake after death scattered it to the east.
I wished I could grope for the spray can in the dark room 8 instead of only being told I couldn't see it.
I wished the guards in 776 gave some audible warning before one walked in to kill me.
I wished the secret stair had pointed me toward where I still needed to go.

lines.line: Footsteps, going away from the brink and coming back to it, the way a man paces who is deciding something, and deciding it in his own favour.
lines.why: It built tension from nothing but sounds. I could feel him deciding whether to leave me there.

lines.line: The water has the look of a cold that would open your hands for you, and would not give back what fell out of them
lines.why: A rule given as a lovely image. I understood exactly what to do.

lines.line: You cannot read the language, but the pictures read you: the flames are leaping up at a window, the statues stand either side of a way, and the old man is waiting.
lines.why: It pointed at the ending and felt slightly menacing.

lines.line: The rock has the look of a thing that has been invited many times.
lines.why: A funny, dry line about the sword in the stone.

lines.line: You slowly remove the hood from your badly wounded opponent and recoil in horror at the sight of your own face, weary and wounded.
lines.why: The emotional peak of the game for me.

lines.line: Three times now I have sent you back, my friend, and the power I spend on you is not in endless store; I do not think there is a fourth in me.
lines.why: A fair warning that I failed to heed, one step before the end.

fun.why: The time machine, the Royal Puzzle and the shadow duel were all great fun to solve. Being killed by the altar and by the guard took some of the fun out.

engagement.why: I always had a clear goal (gather what the old man carries), and each item felt like a step forward. I played 460 turns without getting bored.

difficulty.why: Hard but mostly fair. Missing the ship once and losing the torch across the lake were punishing, unrecoverable mistakes, and the puzzle took a long time to plan.

interestingness.why: Each area works by its own rule: time paradox, sliding walls, a lake that takes your light, a fight you win by sparing. The shadow with my face gave the whole quest meaning.

prose.why: Spare and atmospheric, with dry wit. The added lines about the lake, the cliff man and the old man's fading power were especially good.
